study.title: Ezekiel 11 O Judgment on Jerusalem and hope for the exiles
study.overview: Ezekiel 11 concludes the vision initiated in the previous chapters with two complementary announcements: God judges the leaders of Jerusalem who treated the city as a safe place despite their rebellion, and God comforts the exiles promising to be with them, gather them again and give them a renewed heart. The chapter ends with the withdrawal of the glory of the LORD from the city and with the prophet returning in a vision to Babylon to communicate everything to the captives.

outline.title: Perverse Council on the Eastern Door
outline.explanation: The prophet is taken to the eastern gate of the temple and sees twenty-five city leaders. They represent a government that plans with false security, treating Jerusalem as a guaranteed protection. God answers that this trust is deceptive and commands Ezekiel to prophesy against them.

outline.title: God judges presumptuous and unmasks false security
outline.explanation: The LORD claims to know their thoughts, he accuses the city of violence and announces death, sword and judgment to the border of Israel. The dramatic sign of Pelatias' death confirms the sentence and leads Ezekiel to fear for the survival of the rest of Israel.

outline.title: Promise of presence, meeting and new heart
outline.explanation: God corrects the contempt of the inhabitants of Jerusalem by the exiles and promises to be for them sanctuary in the distant lands. He promises to gather them back, cleanse them from abominations and give them one heart and a new spirit, so that they really live as their people. At the same time, there is judgment for those who persist in desire for abominations.

outline.title: Glory withdraws and the word is taken to the captives
outline.explanation: The cherubim and the wheels move, and the glory of the God of Israel departs from the city and is on the eastern mountain. Then the Spirit takes Ezekiel back to Chaldean, and he communicates to the exiles all that the LORD showed him.

study.context: The chapter is set in the setting of the judgment on Jerusalem and the presence of Jews already taken into captivity. The text shows tension between those who remained in the city and those who were dispersed. The notes point out that the leaders in Jerusalem saw the exiles as far from the LORD and as if the land had been delivered to those who remained, but God corrects this reading: the future of his people was with the exiles, because the LORD himself was with them. No accurate date or secure additional details about the political situation are provided in the notes, in addition to the reference to the Babylonian threat and captivity.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that God knows the thoughts and does not let himself be deceived by religious or political discourses. The false security of the leaders of Jerusalem is judged because it is linked to violence, disobedience and imitation of the surrounding nations. At the same time, God reveals his mercy in accompanying the exiles, becoming sanctuary for them even outside the earth. The promise of the new heart is central: restoration is not only territorial, but internal and moral. God does not just want to gather a scattered people; he wants to form an obedient people, with one heart, living the covenant in which he is their God. The withdrawal of glory shows the seriousness of sin, while the promised return points to God's faithfulness in restoring what was broken.

scholarViews.insight: The wicked counselors trusted the protection of the city as if it preserved them; the note highlights that they defended to stay and build on the taken land, but God had decided to judge them.
The chapter brings a message of anger against those who were in Jerusalem and felt safe, contrasting with the message of comfort to the captives who thought they would never be restored.

The expression of the boiler and the flesh may be a mockery of the previous prophecy, as if they said that destruction would not come so early; the note also links the judgment to the border of Israel.

questions: What false religious or personal security can make us act as the leaders of Jerusalem, ignoring the correction of God?
How does God's promise to be a sanctuary for the exiles confront the idea that the divine presence depends only on one place?
Where today we need the "new heart" promised by God to obey in a concrete way its statutes?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a double call: abandon presumption and embrace the hope that comes from God. Examine whether there are areas where you treat obedience as optional or assume that the current situation protects you. Then ask the Lord to give him a more sensitive heart, able to desire what he desires, and practice a visible obedience at home, at work and in the church. Also learn to comfort others with the promise that God does not abandon those who are in distress, but may be with themselves in distant lands.
study.uncertainty: The notes do not inform with certainty the historical identity of all twenty-five men, nor do they confirm that the names cited in other chapters are the same people; therefore, any more specific association should remain cautious. There is also no exact chronological details or archaeological data on the chapter scenario in the provided notes. The reading of future greetings from the promise of the new heart, although suggested by the notes, should be treated as theological interpretation and not as an explicit statement of the text of this chapter.
